title: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: When we see leaf-eating insects green, and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, and the black-grouse that of peaty earth, we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes”. Scope: animals preyed on by visually hunting predators

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Camouflage has direct, discriminating experimental measures and many reusable datasets. Coverage is insufficient for all animals exposed to visual predators, so the broad scope is only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure visual contrast between prey and natural backgrounds, then relate contrast to detection, attack, survival and heritable colour variation. Lower detection and higher survival for background-matching phenotypes, together with selection on colour, support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Predator visual systems differ from human or camera colour spaces.

Published experimental datasets cover selected conspicuous systems.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data existence: 0.68

discriminating power: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Colour match and predator survival form a clear confirming and refuting contrast, and published experiments already cover insects and a few birds. Those survival data are not gathered in a single downloadable database, and photo archives only proxy the pattern. A compilation could test a familiar subset of visually hunted prey, with serious but manageable alternative functions of colour.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score prey colour against the background where the animal is found, and compare attack rates on matching and mismatched forms by visually hunting predators. Higher survival of matching forms would confirm a protective effect of the tint; equal survival after accounting for temperature and sexual signalling would refute it. Open photo and specimen archives support the match, while the survival contrast lives mainly in individual experiments.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Background matching can serve thermoregulation or sexual display as well as crypsis.

Predation trials that measure the survival benefit are scattered across papers rather than one open table.

Photographs over-represent conspicuous and diurnal animals.

analysis feasibility: 0.46
